## Methods

Chemical and materials
Copper nitrate trihydrate (Ⅱ) (Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, AR), silver nitrate (Ⅰ) (AgNO3, 99.8%), sodium borohydride (NaBH4, 98%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.5%), potassium sulfate (K2SO4, 99%), potassium chloride (KCl, 99.8%), nitrate of potash (KNO3, 99%), Nafion solution (5 wt.%), urea (CO(NH2)2, 99%), iron chloride (Ⅲ) (FeCl3·6H2O, 99%), thiosemicarbazide (MTSC, 98.5%), diacetyl monooxime (DAMO, >98%), sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 95%-98%), phosphoric acid (H3PO4, >85 wt.% in H2O), potassium nitrate-15N (K15NO3, 99%), 15N-urea (CO(15NH2)2, 99%), dimethylsulfoxide-d6 (d6-DMSO, 99.9% D.), sodium nitrite (NaNO2, 99%), sulfonamide (C6H8N2O2S, 99%), N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NETH, 98%), ammonium chloride (NH4Cl, 99.8%), potassium sodium tartrate tetrahydrate (C4H4KNaO6·4H2O, 99%), Nessler Reagent, ethyl alcohol (C2H5OH, 99.9%), nitric acid (HNO3, 65%-68%), potassium hydroxide (KOH, 90%), formaldehyde solution (36 wt.% in H2O), deuteroxide (D2O, 99.9% D.), dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO). All reagents were purchased from Sigma Aldrich Corporation and used without further purification. Carbon papers were purchased from Hesen company (Shanghai, China). High-purity deionized water (resistance 18 MΩ cm-1) were used to prepare aqueous solutions in all experiments.

Synthesis of the AgxCu100-x aerogels
The AgxCu100-x aerogels were prepared via a NaBH4-induced in situ reduction process. Taking the synthesis of Ag67Cu33 aerogel as an example, NaBH4 (50 mM, 25 mL) was homogeneously dissolved in deionized water in the ice-water bath, then the mixed aqueous solutions of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O (50 mM, 1.67 mL) and AgNO3 (50 mM, 3.33 mL) were rapidly dropped into the NaBH4 solution, and the color of the solution turned black instantly. After keeping stirring in the ice-water bath for 1 hour, Ag67Cu33 aerogel was collected by centrifugation and washed with water and ethanol for three times, and finally obtained by freeze-drying procedure. The AgxCu100-x aerogels were acquired using the aforementioned synthetic procedures by varying the molar ratio of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O and AgNO3 (Supplementary Table 2). The pure Ag and pure Cu aerogel catalysts synthesized using the identical method, with the only difference being the addition of either AgNO3 or Cu(NO3)2·3H2O.

The AgCu-mixture catalyst was synthesized by physically blending pure Ag and pure Cu aerogel (obtained from the aforementioned method) in a molar ratio of 2:1, ensuring a homogeneous distribution.

Materials Characterizations
The morphologies of the prepared electrocatalysts were characterized by cold field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, SU8220), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL, JEM-2010). The high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) images and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping images were recorded using a Talox F200X (Thermo Fisher Scientific, America). Atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM was acquired using an aberration-corrected JEM-ARM300F operated at 300 kV. Powder X-ray diffractor (XRD, TTR-III), X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS, Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi) with an X-ray source (Al Kα, hν=1486.6 eV, all the peaks were calibrated with the C 1s spectrum at a binding energy of 284.8 eV), synchrotron radiation X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and Raman spectrometer (LabRam HR) with a 532 nm excitation laser were performed to study the structures and chemical compositions of electrocatalysts. Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer (ICPAES, iCAP 7400) was conducted to determine the element ratios of the catalysts. UV visible photometer (UV-Vis, UV 3600), nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR, AVAVCE III HD 400 and JNM-ECZ600R/SI) and gas chromatograph (GC, GC 7900) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector and TDX-01 column were used for products quantification.

Electrochemical Characterization
The electrochemical measurements were conducted at 25 °C using the CHI660E electrochemical workstation, with continuous injection of CO2 into the electrolyzer or gas chamber during the electrocatalytic process. Data collection and processing were carried out using the Chi660e software. Furthermore, potentiostatic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was utilized to quantify the resistance of the electrochemical cell, ranging from 0.1 Hz to 200 kHz with an applied signal amplitude of 10 mVpp. The pH value of the catholyte was measured using a precision pH meter, revealing that its pH remained consistently at 7.4 ± 0.3 throughout the testing process. Prior to commencing the tests, we prepared the electrolytes (with the precise concentration detailed below) utilizing an electronic scale, beaker, graduated cylinder, and volumetric flask. The mixture was then thoroughly stirred to ensure complete dissolution, achieving a homogeneous solution. Subsequently, it was carefully transferred into a sealed container and stored at ambient room temperature (25 °C) for subsequent experimental use. And the measurements were only performed once. Reference electrode calibration required the immersion of the reference electrode in a buffer solution (pH 7), alongside a glass electrode that had been rigorously calibrated. The open-circuit potential was subsequently measured with high accuracy using pH meter. Calibration was considered successful, and the reference electrode was deemed ready for use only if the deviation between the measured potential and the theoretical reference value (relative to the standard hydrogen electrode at 25 °C with saturated KCl, SCE: +244 mV, Ag/AgCl: +199 mV) was less than 5 mV.

Electrochemical tests in an H-cell
The electrochemical tests in the H-cell were conducted using a three-electrode system, which was separated by a treated Nafion 117 membrane (size: 2×2 cm2, thickness: 183 μm). Before use, Nafion 117 membrane must undergo a pretreatment process: immerse it in a 5% hydrogen peroxide solution at 80 °C for 1 h; rinse it thoroughly with deionized water for 30 min; then soak it in a 5% sulfuric acid solution at 80 °C for 1 h; finally, wash it again with deionized water for 30 min. The catalyst (2 mg) was dispersed in 360 μL of mixture water and ethanol solution (Vwater:Vethanol = 1:1), along with 40 μL of Nafion (5 wt% aqueous solution), through sonication for 20 minutes to form a homogeneous ink. Then 100 μL of the catalyst ink was loaded onto carbon paper and naturally dried to obtain the working electrode. The geometric area of the working electrode was 1×1 cm2, with a catalyst loading of 0.5 mg·cm-2. The anode electrolyte was 0.5 M KHCO3 (35 mL), and a platinum plate electrode served as the counter electrode, while the cathode electrolyte (35 mL) for coupling reactions was CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 with 2000 ppm KNO3 (Ar-saturated electrolyte was composed of 0.5 M K2SO4 with 2000 ppm KNO3). Hg/Hg2Cl2 electrode containing saturated KCl solution was used as the reference electrode. To convert applied potentials to RHE reference scale, ERHE = ESCE + 0.0591×pH + 0.241 formula was utilized, where the pH value was set to 7.4. Before conducting electrochemical tests, the cathode electrolyte was purged with CO2 for 30 min. Subsequently, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements were performed in CO2-saturated electrolyte with KNO3 at a sweep rate of 10 mV/s within the potential range of -0.5 V to -1.5 V (vs. SCE) for 20 min to ensure complete activation of the catalysts. Throughout all electrochemical tests, constant magnetic stirring and CO2 flow rate were maintained.

Urea electrocatalytic synthesis was carried out via controlled potential electrolysis at various potentials for 1 h. The stability test involved continuous controlled potential electrolysis at an applied potential over multiple cycles, with each cycle lasting for 1 hour and refreshing the electrolyte at the beginning of each cycle. Additionally, isotope labeling experiments utilized K15NO3 as a replacement for K14NO3. The electrochemical active surface areas (ECSA) were estimated by calculating the double-layer capacitances (Cdl) from cyclic voltammograms (CV) at scan rates ranging from 40−140 mV/s in a solution of 0.5 M KHCO3 with 2000 ppm KNO3. The differences in current density (Δj = ja - jc) were plotted as a function of the scan rates, and it was determined that the linear slope corresponds to twice the value of Cdl. ECSAs were calculated using the following equation: ECSA = Cdl/Cs, where Cs was the smooth plane capacitance for metal surface (40 μF cm-2)36. The turnover frequency (TOF) of catalysts were calculated using the following formula: TOF = jurea/(16Fn), where jurea was the current density for urea synthesis (A cm-2), F was the Faraday constant (96485 C mol-1), and n was the number of moles of active sites (mol cm-2). CV measurements were conducted at a scan rate of 50 mV/s within the potential range of 0-0.5 V (vs. RHE) in a 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution containing 2000 ppm KNO3. The value of n was determined using: n = Qs/F, where Qs was the surface charge density (C cm-2). By integrating the charge of CV curves, Qs was obtained as half of the integrated value.

Electrochemical tests in a three-electrode flow cell
For the electrochemical tests in a three-electrode flow cell separated by an anion exchange membrane (size: 2×2 cm2, thickness: 100 μm), Ag67Cu33, Nickel foam, Ag/AgCl filled with saturated KCl were employed as the working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. Notably, the anion exchange membrane must be subjected to a pretreatment process, which involves sequentially immersing it in 1 M HCl for 1 h, followed by rinsing with deionized water until neutrality. Subsequently, it should be immersed in 1 M NaOH for 1 h, followed by a thorough rinse with deionized water. 4 mg of catalyst was dispersed in a mixture of 360 μL water and ethanol solution (Vwater:Vethanol = 1:4), along with 40 μL of Nafion (5 wt% aqueous solution). The working electrode (1×1 cm2), loaded with 1 mg·cm-2 was prepared following the same procedure as before. The anode electrolyte remained as 0.5 M KHCO3, but the cathode consisted of 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 with 0.5 M KNO3 (Ar-saturated electrolyte comprised of 0.5 M K2SO4 with 0.5 M KNO3). And electrolytes (35 mL) were continuously injected into their respective compartments during the electrocatalytic process using a peristaltic pump. The applied potentials were converted to the RHE reference scale by ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.0591×pH + 0.197, where the pH value was 7.4. LSV measurements and controlled potential electrolysis remained consistent with those used in the H-cell. The long-term stability test consisted of continuous controlled-potential electrolysis under an applied potential for specific cycles; each cycle lasted 3 h and involved refreshing the electrolyte at the beginning of the cycle.

Electrochemical tests in a two-electrode flow cell
For the FOR/urea synthesis systems, Ag67Cu33 was utilized as the working electrode in both the cathode and anode of the two-electrode flow cell. Subsequently, 35 mL of 1 M KOH (with 0.6 M HCOH) and 35 ml of 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 (with 0.5 M KNO3) were introduced into the anode and cathode compartments at a flow rate of 16 rpm min-1 by a peristaltic pump, respectively, with separation provided by an anion exchange membrane (size: 2×2 cm2, thickness: 100 μm). A catalyst dispersion consisting of 4 mg dispersed in a mixture solution of water and ethanol (Vwater:Vethanol = 1:4), along with 40 μL of Nafion (5 wt% aqueous solution) was prepared. The working electrode (1×1 cm2) loaded with 0.5 mg·cm-2 was obtained using the same procedure as before. Subsequently, both the cathode and anode electrodes required full activation through LSV measurement in the H-cell using previously mentioned methods. Then LSV curves under different conditions in the two-electrode flow cell was measured from 0 V to 2 V at a sweep rate of 50 mV/s. The performance of Ag67Cu33 as a dual-function catalyst was evaluated through constant-current electrolysis at various current densities for 30 min. The cycling tests were conducted at 40 mA cm-2 by ten continuous electrocatalytic experiments, where each cycle lasted 1 h. Subsequently, a long-term stability test was carried out for 60 h at 40 mA cm-2, with the electrolyte being refreshed every 10 h. In all electrochemical tests, after each electrolysis cycle, the electrolytes in the anode and cathode compartments were completely removed via pumping and subsequently replaced with fresh electrolytes before initiating the next cycle.

In-situ Raman measurements
In-situ Raman spectroscopy measurements were conducted with a Renishaw inVia Confocal Raman Microscope equipped with a 532 nm laser (2.5 mW) and an 1800 lines/mm grating, using an Olympus 50X long working distance objective lens (N.A. = 0.5). The electrochemical cell (Supplementary Fig. 32) employed Ag67Cu33 (loaded on 1×1 cm2 carbon paper) as the working electrode, with Pt wire and Ag/AgCl serving as counter and reference electrodes, respectively. A CHI660E electrochemical workstation controlled the system under CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 with 2000 ppm KNO3, with continuous injection of CO2 during the process. Initially, to simulate the activation process, time-dependent Raman spectroscopy measurements were conducted for 20 min using Linear Sweep Voltammetry (LSV). Subsequently, programmed applied potentials were applied for 300 seconds. Simultaneous spectral acquisition (100−1800 cm-1 range) was performed with 15 accumulations per spectrum to monitor any changes occurring within the catalyst material.

In-situ SR-FTIR measurements
In-situ SR-FTIR measurements were performed at National Synchrotron on Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) BL01B beamline using a test reflector with ZnSe window. The equipment setup integrated a KBr beamsplitter-equipped FTIR spectrometer with liquid nitrogen-cooled MCT detectors, coupled to a Bruker Hyperion 2000 microscope with a ×15 magnifying objective lens. Initially, a micrometer-thick gap between the catalyst electrode and the ZnSe window allowed for reflection observation mode to precisely locate the sample’s surface. Subsequently, measurements were performed using vertically incident infrared light in reflection mode. Spectra were acquired with 128-scan averaging at 4 cm-1 resolution, when the source’s beam current exceeded 400 mA.

Background spectrum was first recorded at open circuit potential (OCP). Electrocatalytic measurements applied sequential potentials from -0.22 to -0.62 V vs. RHE (0.1 V increments) and maintained for 200 s. Importantly, the instrument would automatically subtract OCP-derived backgrounds from test results.

Product quantification
The liquid product analysis employed UV-vis spectrophotometry and 1H NMR spectroscopy, while gas-phase quantification was conducted via GC. The specific detection methods are detailed as follows:

Determination of urea
The urea products were determined using the diacetyl monoxime method. Firstly, 60 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid and 20 mL of concentrated phosphoric acid were slowly added to 120 mL of deionized water. Then 33 mg of FeCl3·6H2O was added and the solution was stirred to form a homogeneous solution (Solution A). Secondly, 500 mg of diacetyl monooxime (DAMO) and 10 mg of thiosemicarbazide (MTSC) were dissolved in 100 mL of deionized water to create a uniform solution (Solution B). Thirdly, 950 μL of deionized water, 50 μL of electrolyte, 2 mL of Solution A and 1 mL of Solution B were sequentially added into a glass bottle. The covered glass bottle containing the mixed solution was then heated to 100 °C for 30 min. After cooling down to 25 °C, the absorbance at 525 nm was measured. Notably, the electrolytes in the H-cell were measured directly, whereas the electrolytes in the flow cells were analyzed following appropriate dilution (50 μL of electrolyte in 950 μL of deionized water). The principle and standard curves of diacetyl monoxime method were shown in Supplementary Fig. 25.

The equation of urea yield rate and Faradic efficiency:
Yield rate (mmol h-1 g-1 cat.) = (Curea (μg mL-1) × V(mL)) / (60.06 × t(h) × m(mg))
FE (%) = (16 × F × Curea (μg mL-1) × V(mL)) / (60.06 × Q) × 100
where Curea = generated urea concentration, V=electrolyte volume, t=reaction time, m=catalyst mass, F=Faraday constant (96485.34) and Q = applied electric quantity.

Determination of ammonia (NH3)
NH3 concentration was determined using Nessler’s reagent spectrophotometry. Briefly, 1 g of potassium sodium tartrate (C4H4KNaO6) was dissolved in 2 mL of deionized water to form homogeneous solution. Then 4.9 mL of deionized water, 100 μL of electrolyte, 0.1 mL of potassium sodium tartrate solution and 0.1 mL of Nessler reagent were added to a glass bottle, respectively. Keeping the mixture at 25 °C for 20 min, its absorbance was then measured at a wavelength of 420 nm, as depicted in Supplementary Fig. 27. The equation for the Faradic efficiency of NH3 was as follows:
FE (%) = (8 × F × CNH3 (μg mL-1) × V(mL)) / (17 × Q) × 100
where CNH3 = generated NH3 concentration, V=electrolyte volume, F=Faraday constant (96485.34) and Q=applied electric quantity.

Determination of NO2--N
Nitrite (NO2-) was detected via N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (NETH) spectrophotometric method. The chromogenic reagent was prepared by dissolving 0.4 g of sulfanilamide, 0.02 g of NETH and 1 mL phosphoric acid (ρ=1.70 g·mL-1) in 5 mL of deionized water. Then a mixture comprising 4.9 mL of deionized water, 100 μL of electrolyte, 0.1 mL of chromogenic reagent was added in a glass bottle, and kept at 25 °C for 20 min. The UV-Vis absorption spectra were obtained at a wavelength of 540 nm, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 28. The equation for the Faradic efficiency of NO2-:
FE NO2- (%) = (2 × F × CNO2- (μg mL-1) × V(mL)) / (46 × Q) × 100
where CNO2- = generated NO2- concentration, V=electrolyte volume, F=Faraday constant (96485.34) and Q=applied electric quantity.

Determination of HCOOH and CH3OH
The identification and quantification of formic acid (HCOOH) and methyl alcohol (CH3OH) were performed using 1H NMR spectroscopy. A mixture containing 300 μL of electrolyte, 200 μL of D2O and 100 μL of DMSO (used as an internal standard) was thoroughly blended and subsequently analyzed using the Ascend 400 NMR spectrometer with accumulating 16 scans, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 30. In view of the disproportionation reaction of HCOH (Cannizzaro Reaction, 2HCHO + OH- → CH3OH + HCOO-) occurring in the presence of OH-, which resulted in the spontaneous formation of HCOOH, the concentration of HCOOH generated through the Ag67Cu33-catalyzed FOR at the anode was calculated using the following formula:
CHCOOH (mmol L-1) = CHCOOH-t - (CCH3OH-t - CCH3OH-0)
where CHCOOH-t and CCH3OH-t represented the concentrations of HCOOH and CH3OH in the post-electrolyte as determined by 1H NMR analysis, and CCH3OH-0 denoted the initial concentration of CH3OH in a 0.6 M HCOH solution (without any treatment). By quantifying the amount of CH3OH generated, we could deduce the quantity of HCOOH formed via the spontaneous decomposition of HCOH based on the chemical equation, which allowed for the accurate calculation of the HCOOH produced via the FOR process catalyzed by Ag67Cu33. Notably, the concentration of CH3OH to inhibit the spontaneous polymerization of HCOH, which must be measured beforehand.

Subsequently, the yield rate and Faradaic efficiency of HCOOH achieved using the Ag67Cu33 catalyst via the FOR process were calculated based on the following equations:
Yield rate HCOOH (mmol h-1 mg-1 cat.) = (CHCOOH (mmol L-1) × V(L)) / (t(h) × m(mg))
FE (%) = (1 × F × CHCOOH (mmol L-1) × V(L)) / Q × 100
where CHCOOH represented the concentration of HCOOH produced by Ag67Cu33 catalyst at the anode, V denoted the volume of the electrolyte solution, t indicated the reaction time, m referred to the mass of the catalyst, F Faraday constant (96485.34), and Q signified the charge.

Determination of H2 and CO
Gas-phase products (H2, CO) were analyzed using GC employing high-purity N2 as the carrier gas, with quantification based on calibration-derived conversion factors from standard reference gases (Supplementary Fig. 29). The equation for the Faradic efficiency of H2 and CO:
FE (%) = (2 × F × CH2 (mmol L-1) × V(L)) / Q × 100
FE (%) = (2 × F × CCO (mmol L-1) × V(L)) / Q × 100
where CH2 = generated H2 concentration, CCO = generated CO concentration, V=total volume of the collected gas, F=Faraday constant (96485.34) and Q=applied electric quantity.

1H NMR method and 15N isotope-labeling experiment
The quantification and identification of urea were accomplished via 1H NMR method and 15N isotope-labeling experiment, respectively. For 1H NMR analysis, 400 μL post-test electrolyte (-0.52 V vs. RHE) was mixed with 200 μL dimethylsulfoxide-d6 (internal standard), and analyzed on an Ascend 600 NMR spectrometer (accumulation of 512 scans). Additionally, various concentrations of 14NH2CO14NH2 mixed uniformly with 200 μL dimethylsulfoxide-d6 were used to construct a standard curve for urea quantification. For the 15N isotope-labeling experiment, CO2-saturated electrolyte with 2000 ppm 15KNO3 was utilized, followed by collecting post-test electrolyte at -0.52 V vs. RHE. The isotope-labeled products were detected through the aforementioned 1H NMR method, with 15NH2CO15NH2 solutions serving as isotopic reference.

Computational detail
All calculations in this study were performed using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) based on density functional theory (DFT)52. Projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials and the semi-local generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional were employed53. An empirical dispersion-corrected DFT method (DFT-D3) was applied to accurately describe weak long-range van der Waals (vdW) interactions54. The kinetic energy cutoff for the plane-wave expansion was set to 500 eV, and the convergence threshold for the self-consistent field (SCF) iteration was set to 10-5 eV. Geometry optimization was performed using the conjugate gradient method, with forces on each atom being less than 0.03 eV Å-1. A 1×1×1 Gamma k-point mesh was used for k-space integration. For the adsorption model, a vacuum region of approximately 25 Å was added between slabs to prevent interaction between periodic images.

For the Cu(111) and Ag(111) models, 4×4 supercells with 4 atomic layers were used and two bottom layers were fixed. To simulate the interface between Ag(111) and Cu(111), a heterojunction structure of AgCu(111) was constructed, consisting of a (3×7) Ag(111) supercell with 4 atomic layers and a (3×8) Cu(111) supercell with 4 atomic layers. After fixing the z-axis to optimize the lattice and atomic coordinates, the resulting configuration was considered the final structure of the AgCu(111) model, which was then used to study its C-N coupling properties.

To investigate the effect of electrode potential on the C-N coupling process, the CP-VASP code55,56 was employed, with an external potential of -0.96 V (vs. SHE) and a pH of 7.4. Using the conversion relationship between RHE and SHE, the potential relative to RHE was calculated to be -0.52 V, which aligned with the voltage used in the experiment. Since the TARGETMU value corresponding to the vacuum level was -4.57, the applied voltage and pH conditions led to setting TARGETMU to -3.61, and FERMI CONVERGE was set to 0.01.

Implicit solvation was treated using VASPsol++57, which incorporated water solvation in a self-consistent continuous model. The relative permittivity was set to 78.4 to simulate the water electrolyte. The relationship between the Fermi level (EF) and the corresponding electrode potential, referenced to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) scale U (V vs. SHE), was formulated as follows:
U (V vs SHE) = -4.57 V - EF / e

The grand canonical energy (GCE) was calculated using the formula below:
GCE = E0 + (CNNE - n) * (-eU)
where E0 was the standard VASP output energy, CNNE was the charge-neutral electron number, n was the electron number, and U was the external electrode potential. The grand canonical energy (GCE) was expressed in terms of eV. Note that E0 did not account for changes in the electron number and was no longer an accurate representation of the system’s total energy.

The change in reaction free energy could be obtained using the following equation:
ΔG = ΔGCE + ΔZPE - TΔS + n1*PH*kB T ln 10 + n2 * eU
where ΔGCE was the total grand canonical energy difference before and after intermediate adsorption, ΔZPE represented the difference in zero-point energy, ΔS was the difference in entropy, kB was the Boltzmann constant, and T was the temperature, taken as 298.15 K. n1 was the number of proton transfers involved in the corresponding step, and n2 referred to the number of electron transfers. The pH value used in this study was set to 7.4, and U was -0.96 V. The zero-point energy and entropy of free molecules and adsorbates were obtained from vibrational frequency calculations. Since VASP could not accurately describe charged systems, the energy of NO3- needed to be measured according to this literature58.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this research, the authors developed AgCu biphasic aerogel catalysts with an analogous rectifying interface, which effectively facilitated the synthesis of urea via the coupling reaction of CO2 and NO3-, achieving an ultrahigh urea yield rate (54.8 mmol h-1 gcat.-1) with a Faradaic efficiency (36.6%) at a low potential (-0.52 V vs. RHE). In-situ characterization and theoretical calculations revealed that the analogous rectifying interface effect could generate stable Cuδ+ active sites near the interfaces, thereby enhancing the adsorption of *NOH and stabilizing the *CO intermediate, which improved the C-N coupling dynamics between *CO and *NOH. Furthermore, the two-electrode flow cell utilized Ag67Cu33 as a dual-function catalyst, demonstrating remarkable efficacy in the production of both urea and HCOOH, which underscored its practical applicability. The manuscript is well-structured and presents compelling findings regarding urea production. I recommend the acceptance of this manuscript after minor revisions. Below are some comments for the authors:
1.The authors introduced the concept of “analogous rectifying interface effect” in this study, and chose silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) as the interface materials. Can you provide detailed explanation on this “effect”, and clarify the rationale behind the selection of Ag and Cu for this study?

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors constructed AgCu biphasic aerogels to promote urea synthesis from the co-reduction of NO3- and CO2. The results showed that the proposed exhibit high catalytic performance. Since I am a researcher engaged in theoretical computational work, I will present my question solely from the perspective of density functional theory.
1) According to a recent similar work (Nature Communications 2024, 15, 10331), the similar AgCu biphasic heterostructure exhibits high catalytic performance for producing multicarbon products. However, the urea synthesis and CO2 reduction may compete with each other, which may affect the selectivity of this catalyst. Therefore, the authors should evaluate the selectivity of this catalyst through theoretical calculations, such as its catalytic activity for hydrogen evolution reactions, nitrate reduction, and CO2 reduction to multi-carbon products.
2) C-N coupling is a central challenge in urea synthesis, as it is crucial to the kinetics of the reaction. However, the study does not delve deeply enough into this issue. As mentioned in the paper, different nitrogen-containing intermediates, such as NO and NOH*, are generated during the nitrate reduction process, but the author only considers the coupling between NOH* and CO. While this coupling may indeed be experimentally observed, to highlight the superiority of this coupling, the interactions between other nitrogen-containing intermediates and CO or CO2 should also be considered. More importantly, the author mentions that this coupling can occur spontaneously, which may be inaccurate, as this explanation is solely based on thermodynamics. The author has not calculated the kinetic barriers for these reactions, and therefore, this aspect should also be investigated.
3) The author claims that the formation of AgCu heterojunctions facilitates the reduction of CO2 to CO. However, theoretical calculations show that the Gibbs free energy for this process is as high as 1.27 eV, which is higher than the 0.99 eV for traditional Cu catalysts. This contradicts the experimental results. I suspect this may be related to the CHE model used in the calculations, as this model does not account for the effects of pH and potential, and the author also neglects the influence of solvent effects.
4) The author considers the impact of pH on catalytic activity in the computational method, with a selected pH value of 7. However, the CHE model oversimplifies the influence of pH on catalytic activity, often yielding results that contradict experimental observations. For detailed discussion, please refer to a series of articles by Zhiyao Duan et al. on calculating under constant potential. Therefore, to better account for the effect of pH, we suggest re-evaluating the results using the constant potential method.

1.The authors introduced the concept of “analogous rectifying interface effect” in this study, and chose silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) as the interface materials. Can you provide detailed explanation on this “effect”, and clarify the rationale behind the selection of Ag and Cu for this study?
Author response: We would like to extend our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for raising this pivotal question. As widely acknowledged, copper (Cu) has long been recognized as one of the most promising catalysts for urea synthesis due to its exceptional performance in both carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) and nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR). Extensive prior research had demonstrated that Cuδ+ sites were particularly advantageous active sites for these reactions, as they could modulate the adsorption behavior of intermediates (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 26133-26143; Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2409697). However, maintaining Cuδ+ under applied negative potentials during reduction reactions posed significant challenges, leading to suboptimal catalyst stability. Drawing inspiration from the rectifying interface effect observed in heterojunctions, we hypothesized that constructing a built-in electric field could potentially address this issue. Nevertheless, the regulation of electron redistribution at heterointerfaces was a complex process, influenced by multiple factors including work functions, band structures, and dielectric constants, which were critical in determining the formation of the built-in electric field but were also susceptible to external perturbations. Consequently, we proposed substituting the semiconductor with another metal to achieve an analogous rectifying interface effect. This method facilitated electron transfer across interfaces via the electronegativity differences between metals, offering greater controllability.
In consideration of the exceptional properties and facile synthesis method of bimetallic aerogels, we selected Ag and Cu as the constituent materials. Cu was identified as the active sites for urea synthesis due to its established reputation as an ideal catalyst. The selection of Ag as the secondary metal was motivated by several key factors: firstly, its unique capability to form aerogels, a property shared by only approximately 10% of metals in the periodic table, predominantly precious ones (Matter 2021, 4, 54-94); secondly, its thermodynamic immiscibility with Cu facilitated the formation of critical interfaces, which was crucial for the desired effect; thirdly, its higher electronegativity promoted the induction of Cuδ+, thereby enhancing the catalytic activity; fourthly, its superior electrical conductivity and remarkable stability were essential during the electrocatalytic process; finally, its relatively lower cost compared to other potential metals rendered it a pragmatic choice. In summary, by incorporating Ag as the secondary metal, we had successfully constructed analogous rectifying interfaces with Cu, enabling precise control over electron redistribution and stabilizing Cuδ+, thus significantly enhancing the urea synthesis efficiency.
2.In this study, the authors synthesized a series of AgCu catalysts and evaluated their performance in urea synthesis, and the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) was measured to investigate their electrocatalytic activity. Can you provide the turnover frequency (TOF) in addition to Cdl for a more comprehensive analysis of the intrinsic catalytic activity?
Author response: We would like to extend our heartfelt thanks to the reviewer for their valuable and professional suggestions. To gain a deeper understanding of the intrinsic catalytic activity of AgxCu100-x catalysts, we evaluated the turnover frequency (TOF) of each catalyst. The TOF signified the rate of electron consumption per unit time at an individual active site (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 64, e202413534) and was determined using the following formula: TOF = jurea / (16Fn), where jurea was the current density for urea synthesis (A cm-2), F was the Faraday constant (96485 C mol-1), and n was the number of moles of active sites (mol cm-2). Additionally, n was determined via the formula: n = Qs / F, where Qs was the surface charge density (C cm-2). To obtain these values, cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted at a scan rate of 50 mV/s within the potential range of 0-0.5 V (vs. RHE) in a 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution containing 2000 ppm KNO3. By integrating the charge of CV curves, we obtained the Qs as half of the integrated value, from which we derived the values of n and subsequently the TOF for each catalyst.
As illustrated in Figure S15, the calculated Qs values for Ag, Ag80Cu20, Ag67Cu33, Ag50Cu50, and Cu were 3.95 × 10-5, 1.033 × 10-4, 1.17 × 10-4, 9.97 × 10-5, and 6.38 × 10-5 C cm-2, respectively. Subsequently, the corresponding n values were determined to be 4.09 × 10-10, 1.07 × 10-9, 1.21 × 10-9, 1.03 × 10-9, and 6.61 × 10-10, indicating that Ag67Cu33 possessed the highest number of active sites under identical catalyst loading conditions, which was consistent with the ECSA results. Furthermore, the TOF values of various AgxCu100-x catalysts were compared in Figure S15f, revealing that Ag67Cu33 exhibited the largest TOF value across the entire applied potential range. In conjunction with the ECSA findings, both results confirmed that Ag67Cu33 demonstrated superior intrinsic catalytic activity, thus enhancing urea synthesis performance. Author response: We extend our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for highlighting this intriguing question. We had synthesized a series of AgxCu100-x catalysts and evaluated their performance in urea synthesis, noting significant variations (Figure 2c). According to our density functional theory (DFT) calculations, Cuδ+ sites adjacent to the interfaces served as the active centers for urea synthesis, supported by previous studies. For CO2RR, research on Cu+-rich ultrathin two-dimensional Cu2O nanosheets had demonstrated that Cu+ enhanced the adsorption capacity of *CO (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 26133-26143). In NO3RR, it had also been observed that Cuδ+ facilitated rapid reduction from NO3- to NH3 (Appl. Catal. B Environ.317, 121811 (2022)). More importantly, recent studies on urea synthesis had confirmed that stable electron-deficient Cu played a pivotal role in enhancing urea synthesis efficiency (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202410938; Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2409697).
Therefore, we proposed that the initial increase and subsequent decrease in urea synthesis performance with rising Cu content could be attributed to the fact that the number of Ag-Cu interfaces did not proportionally increase with higher Cu content. This resulted in the actual active sites (Cuδ+) for urea synthesis not genuinely increasing but rather the number of Cu0 sites increasing, leading to more by-products as shown in Figure S9. Consequently, the volcano-like trend in urea synthesis performance for AgxCu100-x could be ascribed to fluctuations in the number of Cuδ+ active sites.
Furthermore, the ECSA (Figure S14) and TOF (Figure S15) results demonstrated that Ag67Cu33, which exhibited the highest performance, also possessed superior intrinsic catalytic activity for urea synthesis, thereby further validating our conclusion.

Author response: We would like to extend our heartfelt gratitude to the reviewer for raising this critical question. It is widely acknowledged that parallel competitive reactions, such as the carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR), nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR), and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) would significantly compromise the efficiency of urea synthesis. While Zhang et al. successfully synthesized an Ag-Cu biphasic heterostructure exhibiting remarkable catalytic performance towards C2+ products (Nat. Commun.2024,15, 10331), it was noteworthy that their required applied potential was more negative than -0.7 V vs. RHE. In contrast, the potential range utilized in our work spanned from -0.22 V to -0.62 V vs. RHE. The different potential window may result in the coupling of N- and C-intermediates or their undergoing further hydrogenation independently (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1095). Furthermore, their research also demonstrated that the Ag:Cu ratio exerted a significant influence on the predominant products, with an observed shift from C2+ compounds to CO as the proportion of Ag increases. To investigate the selectivity of the catalyst, we first evaluated the performance of Ag67Cu33 towards CO2RR using a CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte, which indicated that only CO and H2 were produced, confirming the absence of any C2+ products in our work (Figure S16). Furthermore, the current density observed during the co-reduction of CO2 and NO3- was significantly higher than that achieved in their individual reduction processes, suggesting a potential coupling process.
To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex factors, we conducted DFT calculations on HER, NO3RR, and CO2-to-C2+ processes over the Ag(111)-Cu(111) (Ag67Cu33) aiming to elucidate these in greater detail. Initially, we investigated the synthesis of urea on Ag67Cu33 (Figure S34) from the adsorption of CO2 and NO3-, while also examining their respective hydrogenation pathways in CO2RR and NO3RR, which demonstrated that C-N coupling occurred preferentially, leading to the urea formation, with the rate-determining step (RDS) being the adsorption of NO3-. Notably, the crucial C-N couplings were not only thermodynamically spontaneous but also kinetically favorable. As depicted in Figure S46a, Ag67Cu33 exhibited a preference for *NOH intermediate in NO3RR, where *CO + *NOH formed critical *CONOH intermediate during urea synthesis. Specifically, after CO2 adsorption, both the thermodynamic energy barrier (Figure S34) and the transition state (TS) energy barrier (Figure 35) for C-N coupling (*NOH + *CO → *CONOH) were lower than those for the protonation of *NOH (*NOH + *CO → *NHOH + *CO), which favored the selective occurrence of C-N coupling over NO3RR. For HER (Figure S46b), the RDS involved the desorption of H2 with an energy barrier of 0.94 eV, which was higher than that of the RDS in C-N coupling (0.88 eV), thereby reducing the competitiveness of HER process.
Next, we explored the directed hydrogenation and C-C coupling within the CO2-to-C2+ process (Figure S49). It was evident that the transformation of CO2 + CO2 into *CO + *CO was favored over other protonation pathways and C-C couplings. Notably, the subsequent step required an energy input of 0.28 eV to form *CO + *CHO, and a significantly higher free energy barrier of 0.89 eV to generate *COCO (highlighted in pale pink). However, *CO also emerged as the critical C-intermediate for the first C-N coupling, which proceeded downhill with a low TS energy barrier (Figure S34), which rendered it more inclined toward C-N coupling rather than the protonation of *CO. Following multistep hydrogenation, key intermediates such as *COCH2 and *CHOCH2 were formed, facilitating the production of C2+ products like C2H4 and CH3CH2OH (Nat. Commun.2024,15, 10331; Nature Energy 2024, 9, 1485-1496), while the formation of *CO + *CH4 still remained more facile (indicated in light blue). Although the production of C2+ and hydrocarbons was theoretically feasible, it necessitated multiple hydrogenation and deep reductions, requiring potentials (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., e202503417;Appl. Catal. B Environ. 2023, 325, 122310) far more negative than those applied in our work. In contrast, C-N coupling occurred more readily which utilized *CO as the reaction intermediate. Furthermore, considering the actual process, NO3- exhibited exceptional water solubility as free ions, while the low solubility of CO2 in water introduced resistance during its transition from the gas phase to the liquid phase and subsequent diffusion to the electrode surface (Chem. Eng. J. 2021, 405, 126975). Although the negatively charged NO3- ions experienced increased electrostatic repulsion against the negatively charged electrode, which made their adsorption slightly more challenging (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202402684), their faster diffusion rate compared to CO2 allowed them to effectively occupy sufficient active sites. Consequently, N-intermediates and C-intermediates could intermingle, thus promoting C-N coupling.
In conclusion, during urea synthesis, HER, NO3RR, and CO2-to-C2+ processes could occur concurrently. Cuδ+ active sites were capable of generating NH3 or C2+ products upon the introduction of either NO3- or CO2 (Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 7383). However, when CO2 and NO3- were introduced simultaneously, C-N coupling became preferential due to several critical factors. For NO3RR, the formation of *NOH was facilitated, and the selection of *NOH + *CO to form *CONOH was more favorable than *NHOH + *CO from both thermodynamic and kinetic perspectives. Regarding HER, the free energy barrier of RDS surpassed that of urea synthesis, thereby suppressing H2 production. For CO2-to-C2+, *CO + *CO demanded considerably higher energy than C-N coupling to enable subsequent protonation or C-C coupling processes, and the synthesis of C2+ species or hydrocarbons involved multiple hydrogenation steps and deep reductions, requiring a far more negative electrochemical potential. Macroscopically, two factors might modulate its catalytic behaviors. First, an optimal potential range could not only enhance protonation but also ensure that the coupling process remained dominant over side reactions. However, excessively negative potentials significantly increased the occurrence of undesired side reactions. Second, the factors influenced the mass transfer rates of CO2 and NO3- (such as the flow rate of CO2 or the concentration of NO3-), which in turn affected the effective adsorption of C-/N-intermediates at active sites. Elevated concentrations of either CO2 or NO3- might competitively occupy more active sites, thereby increasing the side reactions. Please refer to line 391 on page 11 of the revised manuscript.

2) C-N coupling is a central challenge in urea synthesis, as it is crucial to the kinetics of the reaction. However, the study does not delve deeply enough into this issue. As mentioned in the paper, different nitrogen-containing intermediates, such as NO and NOH*, are generated during the nitrate reduction process, but the author only considers the coupling between NOH* and CO. While this coupling may indeed be experimentally observed, to highlight the superiority of this coupling, the interactions between other nitrogen-containing intermediates and CO or CO2 should also be considered. More importantly, the author mentions that this coupling can occur spontaneously, which may be inaccurate, as this explanation is solely based on thermodynamics. The author has not calculated the kinetic barriers for these reactions, and therefore, this aspect should also be investigated.
Author response: We are profoundly grateful to the reviewer for their invaluable and perceptive suggestions and for addressing the misrepresentations in our work. In response to the reviewer's insightful comments, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the coupling trends among all potential reactions in the urea synthesis pathway. As illustrated in Figure S34, we evaluated the urea synthesis process on Ag(111)-Cu(111) (Ag67Cu33), beginning with the adsorption of CO2 and NO3-. Subsequently, each step was systematically assessed for possible couplings between N- and C-intermediates, as well as their respective hydrogenation processes. Notably, our results indicated that the free energy barrier for hydrogenation remained lower than that for coupling, until the critical formation of *CONOH from *NOH + *CO, thereby establishing the first C-N bond, which was consistent with our SR-FTIR findings. Furthermore, our analysis extended to subsequent hydrogenation steps, ultimately leading to the formation of the second C-N bond between *CONH2 and *NO2, resulting in the intermediate *H2NCONO2.
Subsequently, we conducted a detailed investigation into the kinetic barriers associated with two critical C-N coupling reactions to elucidate their propensity to occur from a kinetic perspective. As illustrated in Figure S35, the first C-N coupling step involving *NOH and *CO exhibited a transition state (TS) energy barrier of 0.67 eV, notably lower than the 0.95 eV barrier for the protonation of *NOH. Thereafter, *CONH2 and *NO2 overcame a relatively modest TS energy barrier (0.87 eV), forming the intermediate *H2NCONO2. In contrast, the TS energy barrier for the transformation of *CONH2 + *NO2 into *CONH2 + *NOH was significantly higher (1.37 eV).
Considering the free energy diagram for urea production (Figure S34) and the kinetic barriers for the two C-N couplings (Figure S35) on Ag67Cu33, these C-N couplings were not only thermodynamically spontaneous but also kinetically feasible, rendering them more accessible compared to direct protonation (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2402160; Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 5337). We have thoroughly supplemented these details as well as corrected inappropriate expression in our revised manuscript (please refer to line 351 on page 11 of the revised manuscript).

The following sections provide thorough responses to each of reviewer's inestimable recommendations.
1. How do the specific concentrations of NaBH4 and the reaction conditions influence the formation of the AgCu biphasic aerogels? Could variations in these parameters affect reproducibility or performance consistency?
Author response: We are profoundly grateful for the invaluable and insightful feedback from the reviewer. Based on prior researches on metallic aerogels, we successfully synthesized AgCu aerogels via a NaBH4 reduction process (with a molar ratio of NaBH4 to metal ions set at R/M = 5:1) conducted in an ice-water bath. After approximately 35 minutes, this method yielded black precipitates. The carefully chosen reaction conditions were designed not only to control the reaction rate and ensure the reaction proceeded smoothly, but also toguarantee the complete reduction of metal ions. In accordance with the reviewer's recommendations, we conducted a series of meticulously designed experiments utilizing controlled variables to investigate the effects of reaction conditions, including NaBH4 concentrations, reaction temperature and reaction time, on the structure, morphology and catalytic performance of the synthesized catalysts. To ensure consistency and minimize potential human error, we standardized the preparation of metal ion solutions in all subsequent synthesis experiments, and selected Ag67Cu33 as a representative sample, following a theoretical molar ratio of Ag:Cu at 67:33.
Initially, we conducted an in-depth investigation into the impact of varying NaBH4 concentrations. We systematically adjusted the molar ratio of NaBH4 to metal ions (R/M) across a spectrum from 1:1 to 20:1,specifically including ratios of 1:1, 2:1, 5:1, 10:1, and 20:1. Notably, NaBH4 underwent hydrolysis in neutral water, with its rate significantly accelerating as temperature rose. The detailed reactions proceed as follows: NaBH4 → BH4- + Na+, BH4- +2H2O → BO2- +4H2, NaBO2 + H2O → NaOH + H3BO3, which rendered the solution mildly basic and could be catalyzed by metal ions (Ag+ and Cu2+) (J. Saudi Chem. Soc. 2021, 25, 101258). The XRD analysis of catalysts at different R/M ratios, illustrated in Figure R2, revealed that catalysts at R/M ratios of 5:1 and 10:1 exhibited superior crystallinity without any impurities such as Cu2O or Cu(OH)2. SEM images (Figure R3) further confirmed that all catalysts possessed a characteristic three-dimensional reticular aerogel structure, with increasing diameters observed as NaBH4 concentration increased. ICP-MS results (Table R1) indicated a notably lower Cu content at an R/M ratio of 1:1, while a slightly higher Cu content was detected at 20:1. Combining these observations with experimental phenomena, we attributed the observed differences to several possible factors (J. Chem. Educ. 2007, 84, 322; Carbohydr. Polym. 2014, 107, 167-173): when R/M ≤ 2, insufficient BH4- were available to stabilize the reduced metal, leading to rapid aggregation and sedimentation within 15 minutes, resulting in incomplete reduction in the mildly alkaline environment; when 2 < R/M ≤ 10, BH4- effectively facilitated the formation of colloidal metal particles, controlling the aggregation rate and promoting the development of larger diameters and complete reduction; at an R/M ratio of 20:1, the reaction proceeded extremely rapidly within 3 minutes due to the excessive NaBH4, which increased the overall ionic strength and led to aggregation, potentially resulting in partially segregated Ag and Cu (resembling a physical mixture) due to numerous reaction centers with fast rate.

Subsequently, we conducted a series of experiments using an H-cell to rigorously evaluate the catalytic performance of these catalysts in urea synthesis, following a standardized protocol. As depicted in Figure R6, the sample with R/M = 5:1 exhibited superior urea yield rate and Faradaic efficiency compared to others. Considering the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) as indicated by the Cdl values (Figure R11) and the current density (Figure R8), it became apparent that the R/M = 5:1 sample possessed enhanced intrinsic catalytic activity despite a slightly lower current density. Combined with our previous research, this observation indicated that varying concentrations of NaBH4 might significantly influence the formation of Ag-Cu interfaces, which were critical for inducing Cuδ+ active sites for urea synthesis. Furthermore, post-test XRD analysis (Figure R13) revealed the absence of oxides or hydroxides across all samples, attributed to the LSV activation prior to testing. SEM images (Figure R14) confirmed the preservation of the aerogel structure. However, samples with R/M ≤ 2 exhibited increased diameters due to their tendency to agglomerate during catalytic reactions, likely driven by their high specific surface energy.

As the reaction temperature increased, the performance of urea synthesis deteriorated, particularly at 50 ℃ (Figure R7). Although XRD analysis (Figure R15) confirmed that the overall structure remained unchanged after testing when compared to other samples, SEM observations (Figure R15) revealed that particle agglomeration resulted in an increased particle diameter and partial degradation of the aerogel structure at this elevated temperature. ECSA measurements (Figure R12) indicated a decrease in the Cdl value with rising temperature. In contrast, extended reaction time had little impact on the catalyst's structure, morphology, and catalytic efficiency, as evidenced by consistent results in urea yield, FE, ECSA, XRD, and SEM analyses (Figures R7, 12 and 16). However, under alkaline conditions, it was advisable to limit the duration of the reaction to avoid potential adverse effects (Carbohydr. Polym. 2014, 107, 167-173).
In summary, varying concentrations of NaBH4 significantly influenced the aerogel formation process, which in turn exerted a profound influence on the development of Ag-Cu interfaces, thus resulting in their distinct catalytic behaviors. Additionally, an increase in reaction temperature accelerated the reaction rate, leading to larger particle diameters and potential degradation of the aerogel structure, thereby compromising its catalytic efficiency. The aerogel synthesis was completed within 30 to 40 minutes, so extending the reaction time beyond this period offered minimal benefits, particularly in weakly alkaline environments, where excessive duration was neither advisable nor necessary. Consequently, our investigation had determined the optimal reaction conditions as follows: a ratio of 2 < R/M ≤ 10, a temperature range of 0 to 25 ℃, and a reaction time of 1 to 2 h. Under these conditions, the catalyst's structure, morphology, and catalytic performance were maintained without obvious alteration. Among these, a ratio of R/M = 5:1, conducted in an ice-water bath for 1 hour, was identified as the optimal condition in our work.

2. The LSV figure shows that the reduction starts at nearly -0.1V. Why were specific potential ranges (-0.22 V to -0.62 V vs. RHE) selected for electrocatalysis? Could alternative ranges provide insights into different catalytic behaviours?
Author response: We are deeply appreciative of your feedback regarding the selection of potential intervals, which was a critical aspect in electrochemical testing. Initially, we evaluated the catalysts within an H-cell by applying potentials ranging from -0.22 to -0.72 V (vs. RHE). As shown in Figure R17, the urea yield rate exhibited a volcano-type trend, with the optimal catalyst (Ag67Cu33) achieving peak performance at -0.52 V. Regarding Faradaic efficiency (FE), minimal variation was observed at lower potentials, while beyond -0.52 V, FE showed a downward trend. Corroborated by by-product analysis (Figure S9), this decline might be attributed to the enhanced competitive NO3RR at more negative potentials (Nat. Synth. 2023, 2, 624), thereby diminishing urea FE. Consequently, we narrowed our focus to the interval between -0.22 and -0.62 V (vs. RHE) for urea electrocatalysis.
In response to the reviewer's suggestion that reduction commenced near -0.1 V, we extended our investigation on Ag67Cu33 under applied potentials ranging from -0.12 to -0.72 V (vs. RHE) within an H-cell. As illustrated in Figure R18, the production of urea was confirmed even at a potential as low as -0.12 V.However, the urea yield rate was constrained by the relatively low current density. As the potential became increasingly negative, there was a significant escalation in the urea yield rate, along with a moderate increase in FE. The peak urea yield rate (25.7 mmol h-1 gcat.-1) and maximum FE (30.6%) were both achieved at -0.52 V. Subsequently, despite continued increases in current densities, the urea yield rate experienced a slight downturn, paralleled by a marked decrease in FE. In conjunction with the FE of all products (Figure R18c), the catalytic behavior of Ag67Cu33 remained relatively stable at lower potentials. However, at more negative potentials, the increased presence of N-bearing by-products indicated that the accelerated competitive NO3RR likely occupied more active sites (Chem. Eng. J. 2024, 485, 150052; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.63, e202406515), which resulted in a reduced FE of urea at higher potentials.

Author response: We are profoundly appreciative of your invaluable suggestions regarding the control experiments that underscore the pivotal role of Ag-Cu interfaces. Initially, we synthesized pure Ag and pure Cu aerogel catalysts using an identical methodology, with the only difference being the addition of either AgNO3 or Cu(NO3)2. Subsequently, we prepared a uniform physical mixture at a molar ratio of 2:1 to synthesize the Ag2Cu1 catalyst devoid of Ag-Cu interfaces (more details in Materials and Methods on page 14 of the revised manuscript). As shown in Figure S52, its urea synthesis performance was significantly inferior to that of Ag67Cu33, with no notable enhancement observed, thereby emphasizing the essential importance of the analogous rectifying interface effect within Ag-Cu biphasic aerogels. Moreover, we conducted additional experiments on pure Ag and pure Cu aerogel catalysts. As depicted in Figures 2c and 2d, all AgCu biphasic catalysts demonstrated markedly superior urea performance compared to pure Ag and pure Cu catalysts, thus confirming the indispensable role of the analogous rectifying interface effect in enhancing urea synthesis. Furthermore, the subpar urea yield rate from pure Ag suggested that the performance enhancement was not attributed solely to the introduction of Ag. Additionally, the Faradaic efficiency (FE) of all potential products (Figure R19) revealed higher FE for NO2- and NH3 on pure Cu, indicating that increased competition from NO3RR diminished urea FE, which aligned with DFT calculation results (Figure S38), suggesting that the analogous rectifying interface effect might mitigate competitive reactions. 4. Additional surface or bulk characterization techniques can be considered (e.g., XANES, EXAFS) to further confirm the oxidation state of Cu and Ag during the electrocatalytic process.
Author response: We sincerely appreciate the insightful recommendations provided by the reviewer concerning supplementary characterization to elucidate the chemical states in AgCu catalysts. In regards to the XPS analysis results of Ag67Cu33 (Figure 1g-h), it was evident that Ag was present in its elemental form with a zero-valent state, while Cu showed a minor oxidation due to exposure to air. Therefore, to investigate the chemical state of Cu during potentiostatic tests, we performed additional ex-situ synchrotron radiation X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) analysis of Ag67Cu33 at the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL), and we would like to acknowledge the support provided by the BL10B in NSRL for the characterization experiments using Synchrotron Radiation.
We evaluated the Ag67Cu33 catalyst following LSV activation and potentiostatic tests (from -0.22 V to -0.62 V). Post-testing, the catalyst was promptly transferred to a 25°C Ar atmosphere for drying, and subsequently characterized using XANES to probe the Cu L-edge (Figure S30a), thereby minimizing potential air oxidation. As illustrated in Figure S30b, the Cu L-edge spectrum recorded at open-circuit potential (OCP) exhibited distinct peaks at 931.9 eV and 951.8 eV, attributed to the 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 states of metallic Cu, while a minor peak indicative of Cu-O coordination was also observed (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 2816; Nat. Catal. 2018, 1, 421-428), likely arising from surface oxidation during the catalyst loading process on carbon paper. Notably, following subsequent electrochemical treatment, the spectral features only exhibited metallic Cu peaks, without oxide signatures. Furthermore, the integration of operando Raman spectroscopy data (Figure S31), XPS results, and Cu L-edge XANES spectra confirmed the preservation of metallic Ag and Cu in Ag67Cu33 during the electrochemical processes. 5. Stability tests show no significant morphological changes, but what about the possible leaching of Ag or Cu? ICP-MS can be used to confirm the absence of dissolved metals for long-term use.
Author response: We are profoundly appreciative of the reviewer for highlighting the potential leaching of the catalyst, which may influence the stability tests. Following the reviewer's insightful suggestions, we conducted additional stability assessments in both three-electrode and two-electrode flow cells (Figure R20). We employed ICP-MS to rigorously analyze the concentrations of Ag and Cu in the post-electrolytes and the catalysts deposited on carbon paper after tests. As shown in Figure S23, a trace amount of Ag and Cu was detected in the post-electrolytes, with the final catalyst mass on carbon paper stabilizing at 0.97 mg (closely aligning with the calculated loss of 0.95 mg from the electrolytes). This indicated minimal loss during the stability tests, starting from an initial catalyst loading of 1 mg. Notably, the molar ratio of Ag to Cu in the post-test catalyst (71.9:28.1) was higher than the initial ratio of Ag67Cu33 (66.6:33.4), consistent with the greater loss of Cu observed in the post-electrolytes. Consequently, we inferred that the primary cause of catalyst loss was attributed to surface oxidation at the open circuit potential (OCP) when refreshing the electrolytes (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 10331). Then under reductive potentials, this surface oxide might dissolve, leading to catalyst loss, which was supported by in-situ Raman spectroscopy results (Figure S31). Similar observations were made at the cathode in the two-electrode flow cell (Figure S59), where the post-test catalyst on carbon paper had a loading of 0.44 mg (Ag:Cu = 74.4:25.6), with more Cu lost in the electrolytes (calculated retention of 0.43 mg). In contrast, the anode exhibited a molar ratio of Ag to Cu in the post-test catalyst on carbon paper (loading 0.43 mg, calculated retention of 0.42 mg) of 69.8:30.2, close to the initial ratio. This indicated that despite formaldehyde (HCHO) having a lower oxidation potential, some catalyst oxidation and dissolution still occurred under anodic conditions (Nat. Commun. 14, 525). Overall, despite a slight leaching of Ag and Cu observed during stability tests, the catalyst did not dissolve rapidly or extensively, and a significant portion remained intact post-testing, thereby preserving its performance throughout the testing period. We attributed this remarkable structural stability to two key factors (Matter 2021, 4, 54-94): firstly, the three-dimensional porous network structure inherent to metal aerogels, which exhibited intrinsic thermodynamic and chemical robustness, rendering it highly suitable for various catalytic applications; secondly, the incorporation of Ag as a secondary metal, owing to its stable chemical properties, significantly enhanced the material's oxidation resistance and mitigated leaching. 7. The pH value of the electrolyte may be varied accompanied with ammonia production (by-product from NO3– reduction). How the catalytic stability can be maintained?
Author response: We express our gratitude for your insightful observations regarding the potential issues stemming from pH fluctuations during the electrolysis process. To comprehensively investigate these pH changes, we conducted a series of measurements on post-electrolyte pH values at various potentials ranging from -0.12 to -0.72 V (vs. RHE) in an H-cell over Ag67Cu33. As illustrated in Figure R21, the initial pH of the 0.5 M CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution (containing 2000 ppm KNO3) was accurately measured at 7.35. Upon applying increasingly negative potentials, the pH values exhibited a slight upward trend but remained below 8, which value was observed in a standard 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (with 2000 ppm KNO3). Notably, as the pH increased under more negative conditions, there was a corresponding rise in NH3 production (Figure R18). Thus, this phenomenon could be attributed to the *NO2 →*NH3 reaction, which rapidly consumed protons and was the principal driver behind the rapid pH alterations during NO3RR (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2304021).
In subsequent experiments, we assessed the pH changes of post-electrolytes in both three-electrode and two-electrode flow cell (Figures R22), revealing the negligible pH variations throughout these stability tests. We attributed this remarkable stability to two key factors: firstly, the applied potential in stability tests was set at -0.52 V (vs. RHE), resulting in only a modest amount of NH3 being generated. More crucially, the continuous introduction of CO2 throughout the process could react with H2O to form carbonic acid (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3), which could subsequently decompose into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions (H2CO3 ⇌ HCO3- + H+). This dynamic equilibrium helped maintain the pH within the range observed in a 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (pH = 8), thereby ensuring that pH fluctuations did not compromise catalytic performance during electrochemical process.

9. Density functional theory (DFT) models are based on specific crystallographic orientations. How would variations in the crystallographic alignment of the Ag and Cu interfaces affect the results?
Author response: We extend our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for their thorough consideration about the crystallographic orientations influencing the results. Previous studies have demonstrated that different Cu facets exhibit varying catalytic activities in CO2 reduction reactions (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 259-269), NO3- reduction reactions (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2023, 62, e202303327) and urea synthesis (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1095). In our work, we observed that Ag(111) and Cu(111) appeared as the strongest peak in XRD pattern, supported by observations from HR-TEM and HAADF-STEM (Figure 1), which were also the thermodynamically favorable facets (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1749). As a result, we selected Ag(111) and Cu(111) as structural models for Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations. According to prior investigations, the surface energy for Cu crystal facets (ACS Nano 2016, 10, 4559-4564) ranked from highest to lowest, was Cu(110), Cu(100), and Cu(111), while the high surface energy was likely associated with highly active sites (Joule 2020, 4, 2562-2598). However, predicting the behavior of Ag-Cu(hkl) with analogous rectifying interface effect on urea synthesis process, which involved complex 16 electron transfers, remained challenging. Therefore, to address the insightful suggestions from the reviewers more effectively, we developed models incorporating various Cu crystallographic orientations with Ag(111) to construct the Ag-Cu interface, based on the understanding that Cu sites served as the active centers in urea synthesis (Figure R23). Subsequently, we conducted DFT calculations on Ag(111)-Cu(100), Ag(111)-Cu(110), and Ag(111)-Cu(111) to systematically evaluate critical steps, including CO2 and NO3- adsorption, the first C-N coupling, and the second C-N coupling, aiming to investigate their influence on catalytic performance.
The computational models including detailed CONTCAR files for catalysts and adsorbed intermediates were in https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28636625.v2 (in Data availability on page 23).
As shown in Figure R22 and Table R3, Ag(111)-Cu(100) and Ag(111)-Cu(110) exhibited significantly reduced adsorption energies for CO2 and NO3-. However, during the first C-N coupling reaction, Ag(111)-Cu(110) required an energy input of 1.54 eV. In contrast, for the Ag(111)-Cu(100) system, both the first and second C-N couplings showed the largest Gibbs free energy change values, suggesting a potential preference for urea synthesis. These results were consistent with Xu's work on DFT calculations regarding the transformation of NO3- + CO2 into urea (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1095). According to previous studies, Cu(100) has been widely recognized for its remarkable ability to produce C2+ products, primarily due to the increased difficulty of *CO desorption, with a relatively lower energy barrier for C-C coupling (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 259-269; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1749). Moreover, Cu(111) favors the formation of C2+ products through the formation of *COOH and *CO (Energy Environ. Sci. 2022, 15, 3968-3977), while Cu(110) shows an intermediate product selectivity (Surf. Sci. 1995, 335, 258-263). The Cu(100) surface not only facilitates the adsorption of CO2, but also maintains an optimal binding strength with *CO, which might enhance *CO surface coverage, thereby promoting efficient coupling reactions. With regard to NO3RR (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2023, 62, e202303327; ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 14417-14427), both Cu(100) and Cu(110) exhibit a notable capacity to reduce the adsorption energy of NO3-. The subsequent step (*NO3 + H+ → *NO3H) shows significantly enhanced thermodynamic favorability on Cu(100) compared to Cu(111). However, as the reaction proceeds, Cu(111) and Cu(100) remarkably facilitate the hydrogenation of *NO2 into *NOH with significantly higher efficiency compared to Cu(110), particularly on the Cu(111). Notably, *NOH was a critical N-intermediate for the first C-N coupling.
In summary, the integration of our DFT results with previous investigations on Cu facets revealed that both Ag(111)-Cu(111) and Ag(111)-Cu(100) exhibited favorable properties for urea synthesis. Notably, Ag(111)-Cu(100) emerged as the most promising candidate due to its reaction sites with enhanced activity, which effectively promoted the adsorption and activation of reactants, and also exhibited remarkable capability in generating and stabilizing key intermediates (*CO and *NOH), while presenting the lowest free energy barrier for two C-N couplings. These advantages would collectively enhance its performance of urea synthesis. Consequently, we predicted the urea synthesis performance ranking as follows: Ag(111)-Cu(100) > Ag(111)-Cu(111) > Ag(111)-Cu(110). However, it is important to note that the higher surface energy of Cu(100) also makes its formation more challenging under normal conditions (Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 1749). To expose specific crystal facets, researchers have developed innovative strategies (Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 3158; Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 3158). Inspired by the insightful suggestion from the reviewer, in the future, we plan to investigate the design of catalysts featuring Cu(100) or Cu(100)-Cu(111) interfaces, with the aim of thoroughly exploring their potential performance.

10. How was the 0.5 M KNO3 concentration determined to be optimal for flow cell experiments? Experiments can be conducted at different concentrations.
Author response: We are deeply appreciative of the reviewer's insightful suggestion that experiments conducted under varying KNO3 concentrations are crucial. In response, we have supplemented the results for Ag67Cu33 at -0.52 V under different KNO3 concentrations in the flow cell, as illustrated in Figure S18. Initially, the electrolyte containing 0.03 M KNO3 (about 2000 ppm) was utilized, while it resulted in suboptimal urea synthesis performance, even inferior to that observed in an H-cell. Previous studies had demonstrated that flow cells could significantly enhance the carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2303902), a finding also supported by our LSV curves (Figure 2b and 3b). Consequently, a higher concentration of KNO3 was deemed necessary to facilitate the C-N coupling reaction in the flow cell. As depicted in Figure S18b, current densities progressively increased with rising KNO3 concentrations. Furthermore, as the concentration of KNO3 increased, Ag67Cu33 exhibited progressively higher urea yield rates along with enhanced Faradaic efficiencies (FE), achieving optimal performance at 0.5 M KNO3. However, further increases in KNO3 concentrations led to a decline in urea synthesis performance, which could be attributed to excessively high KNO3 concentrations inhibiting CO2 adsorption by promoting NO3- adsorption (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 63, e202406515), thereby favoring competitive nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) and consequently reducing both urea yield rate and FE. Therefore, we selected 0.5 M KNO3 for subsequent electrochemical tests in the flow cell. Detailed analysis and discussion of these data are also provided in the main text, specifically from line 243 on page 7 of the revised manuscript.
